newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran police prevent protests at German embassy.
newsitem.headline: Iran police prevent protests at German embassy.

text.p: Iranian police on Sunday prevented two groups of demonstrators from staging protests at the German embassy over allegations that Tehran ordered murders in Germany.

Dozens of police in riot gear stood in three lines to guard the embassy and prevent several hundred workers chanting "Death to Fascists" from holding demonstrations, but they were allowed to march past the mission in central Tehran.
The embassy was closed and callers were told normal business would resume on Monday.

The workers carried banners condemning a German prosecutor who alleged Iranian leaders ordered the 1992 murders of three Kurdish dissidents and their translator in Berlin. They chanted "Death to America" and "Death to Israel".
Another march by several hundred members of the hardline Islamic Ansar-e Hizbollah (Supporters of the Party of God) group was steered away before they could reach the embassy.
They chanted "Germany is the servant of Zionists", "Death to Israel" and "Death to America" and carried a banner saying "We condemn the insults of the German prosecutor".
Ansar-e Hizbollah distributed a leaflet which condemned the "criminal neo-nazi German government".
Tehran bazaar was closed until noon as part of the protest.

The German charges have provoked outrage in Iran, where the government has been trying to ease tensions with its main trade partner. Protesters have rallied outside the embassy, pelting the compound with eggs and tomatoes and calling for the prosecutor to be executed.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said on Friday the German government was under U.S. and Israeli pressure but said he hoped Bonn would prevent tensions from spiralling out of control.
Rafsanjani said Iran hoped to continue its friendship with Germany despite strains over the trial in Berlin of five men for the 1992 killings.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told his Iranian counterpart Ali Akbar Velayati in a telephone call that the German judiciary was independent and that Bonn had no right to interfere in court proceedings.
